title: Velouté de cresson
subtitle: French watercress velouté
excerpt: Vivid green soup made from watercress, leek, and potato, blended until smooth and finished with crème fraîche. Bright in colour and peppery in flavour. Served hot or chilled.
sourceNotes: Velouté de cresson is a classic French soup, closely related to potage cressonnière, which appears in Escoffier's Le Guide Culinaire (1903) and Larousse Gastronomique (1938). Both are available as public-domain or widely-cited historical culinary references.

recipe.freezeNotes: Not suitable for freezing: the watercress loses its vivid colour and fresh flavour on freezing and reheating.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Can be made up to 24 hours ahead and served chilled, or reheated gently. Do not boil after adding the cream.

content.text: Velouté de cresson is spring on a plate. The watercress gives it an insistent peppery sharpness, the leek and potato give it body, and blending it briefly (never for too long, or the colour dulls) keeps the colour a vivid jade green. It is one of the few French soups that works equally well hot and cold. Served chilled before a dinner in May or June, it is as elegant as anything.

items.prepNote: white and pale green parts only, sliced

content.text: Melt the butter in a large saucepan over medium heat. Add the leek and cook gently for 8 minutes until soft. Add the potato and stir to coat.
Pour in the hot stock. Bring to the boil and simmer for 15 minutes until the potato is completely tender.
Add the watercress to the pan. Simmer for exactly 2 minutes. No longer: the watercress must stay bright green. Blend immediately until smooth.

Stir in the crème fraîche. Season with salt and pepper. Serve hot, or cool quickly and refrigerate to serve chilled. If serving chilled, taste and re-season just before serving: cold food needs more salt.

items.symptom: Soup is grey-green rather than vivid green
items.fix: Add the watercress last and blend immediately after 2 minutes. The heat of the blender will cook it further: speed matters here.

items.cause: Underseasoned, or the watercress was not peppery enough
items.fix: Season generously, especially if serving cold. Add a squeeze of lemon juice to brighten it.

content.text: Watercress soup has been a feature of French spring cooking since at least the early twentieth century. In France it is associated with the rivers and chalk streams of Normandy and the Île-de-France, where watercress is farmed in fast-running, cold water. The soup is served both chilled (as a potage froid for a summer dinner) and hot (as a winter first course). Either way, it needs nothing more than a swirl of crème fraîche and a little extra black pepper.
